summary: 7. The present Appeal Nos. 107 of 2019 and 166 of 2020 arise out of proceedings in Petition No. 74 of 2017 decided by the Himachal Pradesh State Electricity Regulatory Commission vide orders dated 21.11.2018 (Impugned Order-1) and 15.05.2020 (Impugned Order-2) (collectively referred to as the “Impugned Orders”). 8. Since both the Appeals emerge from the same petition, involve common parties and raise interconnected issues, they are being decided by this common judgment. 19. Aggrieved by the order dated 16.07.2010, the Appellant preferred Appeal No. 179 of 2010 before this Tribunal. By judgment dated 23.04.2012, this Tribunal, while partly allowing the Appeal, observed that tariff of a hydro project is significantly dependent on water inflows and noted the Appellant’s contention that the actual river discharge was substantially lower than that envisaged at the DPR stage. This Tribunal granted liberty to the Appellant to approach the HPERC with updated and supporting data to establish its case regarding low river discharge and directed the HPERC to consider the same after affording opportunity of hearing to all concerned parties. 22. The Respondent No. 2 filed its reply denying the claims raised by the Appellant-Petitioner, including issue of maintainability of Petition No. 74 of 2017. By interim order dated 21.11.2018, the HPERC rejected the objection as 23. However, HPERC vide interim order dated 21.11.2018 held that the said intervention can be made only prospectively. Aggrieved by this interim order, the Appellant filed Appeal No. 107 of 2019 before this Tribunal. 25. Being aggrieved by the interim order dated 21.11.2018 and final order dated 15.05.2020 passed by HPERC in Petition No. 74 of 2017, the Appellant has preferred the present Appeal Nos. 107 of 2019 and 166 of 2020. 27. According to the Appellant, the Judgment dated 23.04.2012 has attained finality inter se the parties. In particular, the findings recorded in Paras 36 to 38 are binding between the parties. This Tribunal had observed that reliance on one year’s data was inadequate to validate the hydrology of the Project and had acknowledged that lower river discharge than that envisaged at the planning/tendering stage would amount to a change in circumstances and in the basic parameters on the basis of which the Project was developed. The Tribunal had also taken note of the statutory objective of promoting renewable sources of energy under the Electricity Act. 28. The Appellant contends that these findings constitute mixed questions of law and fact and are not pure questions of law. Having attained finality, they operate inter-parties and bind the Respondent. Consequently, the Respondent is precluded from re-agitating the issue and its present contention that the PPA cannot be reopened is barred by the principles of constructive res judicata. 31. The finding of Tribunal is in the nature of factual conclusion which finding has become final and binding upon the parties. Any subsequent judgment, on a pure question of law about re-opening of PPA would thus, not apply to the aforesaid finding of fact, which finding has become final, inter-parties. Therefore, law laid down in Mathura Prasad Bajoo Jaiswal case (1970) 1 SCC 613 would not apply to the facts of the instant case. 34. The Appellant further contends that mere overruling of principles on which earlier judgment was passed by a subsequent judgment of a higher forum will not uproot the final adjudication between the parties. In support, reliance is placed on _Neelima Srivastava vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors. (2021) 17 SCC 693._ 47. The Petition was filed by the Appellant-Petitioner in terms of the liberty granted by the Tribunal in Appeal No. 179 of 2010 dated 23.04.2012. This Tribunal had held as under: 48. In this background of findings, this Tribunal gave liberty to the Appellant to approach the State Commission with relevant hydrological data. 50. Respondent No. 2 submits that the finding of this Tribunal in the earlier round of litigation regarding the power of the HPERC to reopen the PPA were rendered in the context of the legal position prevailing at that time. The Tribunal had, inter alia, proceeded on the footing that HPERC could exercise regulatory 52. It is stated that the doctrine of res judicata is a rule of procedure and cannot be invoked to perpetuate an incorrect legal position. Reference is placed on _Mathura Prasad Badoo Jaiswal vs. Dossibai N.B. Jeejeebhoy, (1970) 1 SCC 613._ 64. We also note that this Tribunal in Patikari-1 Judgment had concluded as under _:_ 65. The above mentioned Judgement has attained finality. While the parties have advanced competing arguments on issue (ii) above as to whether the finding that the Commission has powers to review or modify the PPA operates as _res judicata_ , there is no such dispute in respect of the other three findings. _vii. that because of the abysmally low generation and consequent lower revenues on account of lower discharges in the river on which the Project is located, Petitioner has been put to tremendous financial constraints right since commissioning of its project making it extremely difficult even to service the loans. Many a time since its commissioning the Project has been on the verge of being declared as NPA when the Petitioner had perforce to infuse additional funds from time to time by arranging additional inter-corporate loans or through other means to avoid this.
